By starting with a lightweight stable entry point (`AGENTS.md`) that points to granular, domain-specific sub-documents inside `docs/` on demand, the agent avoids context window overcrowding and preserves high reasoning quality.[^migration-source-harness-engineering-in-an-agent-first-world-0][^migration-source-how-to-build-a-coding-agent-workshop-1][^migration-source-harnesses-eager-vs-just-in-time-2][^migration-source-how-claude-code-uses-prompt-caching-3][^migration-source-hermes-agent-prompt-assembly-4] --- ## 1. Failure of Monolithic Instruction Manuals As documented by [Ryan Lopopolo](../entities/ryan-lopopolo.md) in [Source - Harness Engineering in an Agent-First World](../sources/source-harness-engineering-in-an-agent-first-world.md), the "one big `AGENTS.md`" or `.cursorrules` approach fails for three reasons: 1. **Context Window Starvation**: Massive instruction files consume 20%–40% of the available context window before the agent even reads a single line of codebase source code. 2. **Attention Decay ("Non-Guidance")**: When hundreds of rules are presented simultaneously with equal weight, LLM attention mechanisms fail to prioritize critical architectural constraints over minor formatting preferences. 3. **Documentation Rot**: Monolithic instruction files rot quickly because engineers update individual code modules without refactoring a 3,000-line global prompt file. --- ## 2. Table of Contents (TOC) Architecture: The 3-Tier Hierarchy TOC Architecture structures repository instructions into three modular tiers: ```mermaid flowchart TD classDef tier1 fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px,color:#0d47a1 classDef tier2 fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32,stroke-width:2px,color:#1b5e20 classDef tier3 fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e65100,stroke-width:2px,color:#bf360c T1["TIER 1: Root Index Map (/AGENTS.md)
~50-100 lines max. High-level map linking to domain guides."] T1 -->|"On-Demand Read"| T2A["TIER 2: docs/db/
schema.md"] T1 -->|"On-Demand Read"| T2B["TIER 2: docs/api/
endpoints.md"] T1 -->|"On-Demand Read"| T2C["TIER 2: docs/ui/
components.md"] T2B -->|"On-Demand Read"| T3["TIER 3: Local Override
/src/api/AGENTS.md"] class T1 tier1 class T2A,T2B,T2C tier2 class T3 tier3 ``` ### Tier 1: Root Index Map (`/AGENTS.md`) — (~50 to 100 lines max) The agent boots with a lightweight root file that acts **strictly as a table of contents and directory map**: * High-level repository tree and module descriptions. * 3–5 golden non-negotiable architectural principles. * A clear markdown index mapping subsystems to domain documentation. ### Tier 2: Domain-Specific Sub-Documents (`/docs/...`) Specialized instruction files scoped strictly to a single architectural domain (e.g., `docs/db/schema.md` or `docs/rules/testing.md`). The agent uses [Read Tool](read-tool.md) to inspect these sub-documents **only when its active task requires modifying code in those specific sub-directories**. ### Tier 3: Directory-Scoped Local Overrides (`/src/module/AGENTS.md`) Deeply nested sub-directories contain local `AGENTS.md` files that specify rules unique to that sub-folder (e.g., security guidelines inside `/src/auth/AGENTS.md`). --- ## 3. Core Benefits * **Pruned Context Footprint**: Initial system prompts stay lightweight (~1k tokens), leaving >95% of the context window open for source code, terminal logs, and execution diffs. * **Dynamic Attention Alignment**: The agent only reads and attends to rules relevant to the active module. * **Automated Documentation Gardening**: Modular, single-topic doc files are easy for automated background agents to audit, verify against code diffs, and update via pull requests. --- ## 4. Admission Control Beyond Files Progressive disclosure is one implementation of [Context Admission Control](context-admission-control.md). The same index-and-pointer structure can govern optional skills, MCP tools, memory, and subagents: expose a compact catalog, select entries for the active task, and append the selected detail without rewriting the stable prompt prefix. Claude Code applies this through just-in-time file search and deferred tool schemas. Hermes Agent applies it through a stable/context/volatile prompt assembly and separate ephemeral plugin overlays. In both cases, the key invariant is that changing runtime state should not force a rewrite of durable instructions. ## Related Wiki Pages * [Harness Engineering](harness-engineering.md) * [Coding Agent](coding-agent.md) * [Context Admission Control](context-admission-control.md) * [Claude Code](claude-code.md) * [Hermes Agent](../entities/hermes-agent.md) * [Source - Harness Engineering in an Agent-First World](../sources/source-harness-engineering-in-an-agent-first-world.md) * [Synthesis - Harness Engineering Architecture](../analyses/synthesis-harness-engineering-architecture.md) ## Evidence & Citations - [Source Note](../sources/source-harness-engineering-in-an-agent-first-world.md) - [Source Note](../sources/source-how-to-build-a-coding-agent-workshop.md) - [Source Note](../sources/source-harnesses-eager-vs-just-in-time.md) - [Source Note](../sources/source-how-claude-code-uses-prompt-caching.md) - [Source Note](../sources/source-hermes-agent-prompt-assembly.md) [^migration-source-harness-engineering-in-an-agent-first-world-0]: [Source Note](../sources/source-harness-engineering-in-an-agent-first-world.md), claims matrix; [Raw File](../../raw/Harness%20engineering%20leveraging%20Codex%20in%20an%20agent-first%20world.md). # Synthesis - Code RAG via Tree-sitter and LSP

## Overview & Architecture

Modern AI [Coding Agent](../concepts/coding-agent.md) harnesses (such as Cursor, Claude Code, Antigravity, Aider, and Sourcegraph Cody) avoid naive text-based [Retrieval-Augmented Generation](../concepts/retrieval-augmented-generation-rag.md) (vector embedding chunking every 500 tokens). Instead, they deploy a **dual-engine deterministic Code RAG pipeline** combining **[Tree-sitter](../concepts/tree-sitter.md)** and the **[Language Server Protocol](../concepts/language-server-protocol-lsp.md) (LSP)**:[^migration-source-how-to-build-a-coding-agent-workshop-0][^migration-source-harness-engineering-in-an-agent-first-world-1]

- **[Tree-sitter](../concepts/tree-sitter.md) = Micro-Level Single-File Microscope**: Parses single-file in-memory buffers into Concrete Syntax Trees (CST/AST) in $<1\text{ ms}$, extracts AST-aware chunks, strips function bodies for Tier-2 [Progressive Disclosure](../concepts/progressive-disclosure.md) file outlines, and validates patch syntax.
- **[LSP](../concepts/language-server-protocol-lsp.md) = Macro-Level Workspace Atlas**: Manages cross-file semantic dependency graphs, locates symbol definitions across directories (`textDocument/definition`), tracks call sites (`textDocument/references`), and returns compiler type-checking diagnostics (`publishDiagnostics`).

                                        │

│ 1. Tree-sitter AST Chunker (Micro)      │       │ 2. LSP Symbol Resolver (Macro)          │
│ • Parses local files into AST nodes     │       │ • Queries `textDocument/definition`     │
│ • Extracts function/class bounds        │       │   to locate exact symbol file/line      │
│ • Strips bodies for Tier-2 outlines     │       │ • Queries `textDocument/references`     │
└────────────────────┬────────────────────┘       └────────────────────┬────────────────────┘

                               └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                                                │
                                                ▼
                               ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
                               │ Token-Optimized LLM Prompt      │
                               └─────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Complete Python Implementation Example

The following end-to-end Python script demonstrates how a dual-engine [Code RAG](../concepts/code-rag-code-aware-retrieval-augmented-generation.md) pipeline processes a codebase query by combining `TreeSitterASTChunker` and `LSPClient`:

```python
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Dict, Optional
import tree_sitter_python as tspython
from tree_sitter import Language, Parser, Node

# =====================================================================
# 1. TREE-SITTER ENGINE: AST Chunker & Outline Extractor (Micro Level)
# =====================================================================
@dataclass
class CodeASTChunk:
    name: str
    kind: str  # 'function' or 'class'
    start_line: int
    end_line: int
    signature: str
    full_code: str

class TreeSitterASTChunker:
    """Uses Tree-sitter to perform AST-aware code chunking and signature extraction."""
    
    def __init__(self):
        self.language = Language(tspython.language())
        self.parser = Parser(self.language)

    def parse_file(self, file_path: str, source_code: bytes) -> List[CodeASTChunk]:
        """Parses a file into discrete AST chunks (functions/classes) using S-expressions."""
        tree = self.parser.parse(source_code)
        chunks = []
        
        # S-expression query to capture function and class declarations
        query_scm = """
        (function_definition
          name: (identifier) @func.name) @func.def
        (class_definition
          name: (identifier) @class.name) @class.def
        """
        query = self.language.query(query_scm)
        captures = query.captures(tree.root_node)

        lines = source_code.decode('utf-8').splitlines()

        for node, tag in captures:
            if tag in ('func.def', 'class.def'):
                start_line = node.start_point.row
                end_line = node.end_point.row
                kind = 'function' if tag == 'func.def' else 'class'
                
                # Extract signature vs full code block
                signature = lines[start_line].strip()
                full_code = "\n".join(lines[start_line:end_line + 1])
                
                name_node = node.child_by_field_name('name')
                name = source_code[name_node.start_byte:name_node.end_byte].decode('utf-8') if name_node else "unknown"

                chunks.append(CodeASTChunk(
                    name=name,
                    kind=kind,
                    start_line=start_line + 1,  # 1-indexed for LSP
                    end_line=end_line + 1,
                    signature=signature,
                    full_code=full_code
                ))
        return chunks

    def generate_file_outline(self, source_code: bytes) -> str:
        """Tier-2 Progressive Disclosure: Generates file outline (signatures only, bodies removed)."""
        chunks = self.parse_file("buffer.py", source_code)
        outline = []
        for c in chunks:
            outline.append(f"  Line {c.start_line}-{c.end_line}: {c.signature} ...")
        return "\n".join(outline)


# =====================================================================
# 2. LSP CLIENT: Cross-File Semantic Resolver (Macro Level)
# =====================================================================
@dataclass
class LSPLocation:
    uri: str
    line: int
    character: int

class MockLSPClient:
    """Simulates JSON-RPC client interacting with a Language Server daemon."""
    
    def goto_definition(self, file_uri: str, line: int, character: int) -> Optional[LSPLocation]:
        """Queries textDocument/definition to resolve cross-file symbol targets."""
        print(f"  [LSP Request] textDocument/definition -> {file_uri}:{line}:{character}")
        # Simulated response: UserAuthService is defined in auth_service.py at line 2
        return LSPLocation(uri="file:///workspace/auth_service.py", line=2, character=4)

    def find_references(self, file_uri: str, line: int, character: int) -> List[LSPLocation]:
        """Queries textDocument/references to locate all call sites in the repository."""
        print(f"  [LSP Request] textDocument/references -> {file_uri}:{line}:{character}")
        return [
            LSPLocation(uri="file:///workspace/controllers/user.py", line=45, character=12),
            LSPLocation(uri="file:///workspace/middleware/auth.py", line=18, character=8),
        ]


# =====================================================================
# 3. DUAL-ENGINE CODE RAG PIPELINE
# =====================================================================
class DualEngineCodeRAG:
    """Orchestrates Tree-sitter (local AST) + LSP (global semantics) to build LLM context."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.ts_chunker = TreeSitterASTChunker()
        self.lsp_client = MockLSPClient()

    def assemble_context(self, active_file: str, active_code: bytes, target_symbol_line: int, symbol_char: int) -> str:
        # Step 1: Use Tree-sitter for Tier-2 Progressive Disclosure Outline of active file
        active_outline = self.ts_chunker.generate_file_outline(active_code)

        # Step 2: Use LSP to resolve exact cross-file definition of target symbol
        def_loc = self.lsp_client.goto_definition(active_file, target_symbol_line, symbol_char)

        # Step 3: Fetch target file, use Tree-sitter to slice target function's exact AST node
        target_file_code = b"""
class UserAuthService:
    def validate_token(self, token: str) -> bool:
        \"\"\"Validates JWT token against security secret.\"\"\"
        if not token.startswith("Bearer "):
            return False
        return True
"""
        target_chunks = self.ts_chunker.parse_file(def_loc.uri, target_file_code)
        target_chunk = next((c for c in target_chunks if c.start_line <= def_loc.line <= c.end_line), None)

        # Step 4: Assemble final token-optimized prompt payload
        prompt_context = f"""
=== CODE RAG CONTEXT ===

[Active File Outline: {active_file}] (Tier-2 Outline via Tree-sitter)
{active_outline}

[Resolved Definition: {def_loc.uri}] (Tier-3 Implementation via LSP + Tree-sitter)
File: {def_loc.uri} (Line {target_chunk.start_line}-{target_chunk.end_line})
{target_chunk.full_code}
"""
        return prompt_context


# =====================================================================
# DEMO EXECUTION
# =====================================================================
if __name__ == "__main__":
    sample_active_code = b"""
from auth_service import UserAuthService

class UserController:
    def handle_login(self, request):
        auth = UserAuthService()
        return auth.validate_token(request.headers.get("Authorization"))
"""
    rag = DualEngineCodeRAG()
    context = rag.assemble_context(
        active_file="file:///workspace/controllers/user.py",
        active_code=sample_active_code,
        target_symbol_line=6,
        symbol_char=20
    )
    print(context)
```

---

## Assembled Context Output

The resulting context window payload sent to the LLM agent is concise, structured, and syntactically complete:

```text
=== CODE RAG CONTEXT ===

[Active File Outline: file:///workspace/controllers/user.py] (Tier-2 Outline via Tree-sitter)
  Line 4-7: class UserController: ...
  Line 5-7: def handle_login(self, request): ...

[Resolved Definition: file:///workspace/auth_service.py] (Tier-3 Implementation via LSP + Tree-sitter)
File: file:///workspace/auth_service.py (Line 2-7)
class UserAuthService:
    def validate_token(self, token: str) -> bool:
        """Validates JWT token against security secret."""
        if not token.startswith("Bearer "):
            return False
        return True
```

---

## Architectural Advantages

1. **Syntactic Chunk Integrity**: Traditional text chunking splits files every $N$ tokens, slicing function signatures or indentation blocks in half. [Tree-sitter](../concepts/tree-sitter.md) guarantees every chunk is a complete AST node.
2. **Deterministic Symbol Resolution**: Vector distance search frequently returns irrelevant functions with high keyword similarity. [LSP](../concepts/language-server-protocol-lsp.md) guarantees 100% accurate definition lookups across multi-thousand file repositories.
3. **Token Budget Optimization**: By pairing [Progressive Disclosure](../concepts/progressive-disclosure.md) Tier-2 file outlines with targeted Tier-3 AST node extractions, prompt token consumption drops by 70–90% compared to dumping full files into context.

This failure is driven by three cognitive phenomena inherent to Large Language Models:[^migration-source-make-llm-output-more-reliable-using-verifiers-0][^migration-source-verifier-pattern-in-multi-agent-systems-1][^migration-source-how-to-build-an-ai-agent-from-scratch-in-python-2] 1. **Bias Inheritance**: The builder agent evaluates generated code against the mental representation and assumptions built during generation, confirming its own misunderstandings (e.g. evaluating ascending sort as correct because it misread the prompt as requesting descending sort). 2. **Systematic Blind Spots**: Model errors cluster around specific reasoning patterns (misread edge cases, missing null checks). Re-invoking the same model in the same context re-executes those identical reasoning paths. 3. **Context Window Contamination**: LLMs strongly favor context consistency. Prior reasoning turns bias the model to rationalize existing output rather than challenge it. The **[Verifier Pattern](../concepts/verifier-pattern.md)** solves this by establishing an independent verification layer—either through context-isolated multi-agent review or deterministic compiler/runtime sandboxes. --- ## 1. Dual Verifier Paradigms ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Builder Phase Req[Original Requirements & Spec] --> Builder[🤖 Builder Agent] Builder --> Artifact[Generated Code / Schema Artifact] end subgraph Verification Phase Artifact --> V1["🧠 Inferential Verifier Agent
(Fresh Context Window / Heterogeneous Model)"] Artifact --> V2["⚙️ Computational Verifier Engine
(Compiler / Static Analysis / Lean Theorem Prover)"] V1 --> Audit1{Verdict: Pass or Fail?} V2 --> Audit2{Type-Check & Sandbox Run Pass?} end Audit1 -- Pass --> Prod[Approved Production Output] Audit2 -- Pass --> Prod Audit1 -- Fail --> Loop["Structured Issue JSON
(Line Numbers, Severity, Bug Descriptions)"] Audit2 -- Fail --> Loop Loop --> Builder ``` ### Paradigm A: Inferential Multi-Agent Verifier (Context Isolation) - **Zero Shared Context**: The verifier agent is invoked with a fresh, un-contaminated context window containing *only* the raw requirements and the generated artifact—never the builder's scratchpad, thought chain, or intermediate exploration turns. - **Heterogeneous Model Verification**: Pairing different model families (e.g. GPT-4o builder paired with a Claude 3.5 Sonnet verifier) leverages distinct training sets and reasoning patterns to eliminate single-provider blind spots. ### Paradigm B: Computational & Formal Verifier (Compiler + Runtime Sandbox) - **Compiler Role**: Validates syntactic, structural, and type correctness (e.g., AST parsing, static analysis, or formal proof assistants like [Lean](../entities/lean-proof-assistant.md)). - **Runtime Role**: Executes generated code inside a sandboxed container against synthetic edge cases, property-based tests, or business rules. --- ## 2. Multi-Agent Validation Sequence ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber actor Harness as Agent Harness participant Builder as Builder Agent participant Verifier as Verifier Agent (Fresh Context) participant Sandbox as Execution Sandbox Harness->>Builder: Send Task Requirements Builder->>Builder: Generate Code / Spec Artifact Builder-->>Harness: Return Artifact String Harness->>Verifier: Invoke Fresh Context (Requirements + Artifact Only) Verifier->>Sandbox: Compile & Execute Artifact against Test Cases Sandbox-->>Verifier: Return Execution Logs / Proof Status Verifier->>Verifier: Evaluate Output & Formulate Verdict Verifier-->>Harness: Return Structured JSON Result alt Verdict == Pass Harness->>Harness: Deploy / Commit Verified Code else Verdict == Fail (Retries < Hard Cap) Harness->>Builder: Re-invoke Builder with Structured Issue JSON else Retries >= Hard Cap Harness->>Harness: Escalate to Human Review / Fallback Logging end ``` --- ## 3. Structured Verification Payload Schema Effective verifiers output machine-readable JSON rather than natural language paragraphs, ensuring the builder agent parses exact line numbers and actionable feedback: ```json { "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema", "title": "VerifierResult", "type": "object", "properties": { "verdict": { "type": "string", "enum": ["pass", "fail"] }, "iteration": { "type": "integer" }, "issues": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "object", "properties": { "line": { "type": "integer" }, "severity": { "type": "string", "enum": ["critical", "warning", "info"] }, "category": { "type": "string", "enum": ["syntax", "type_error", "logic", "security", "boundary"] }, "description": { "type": "string" }, "suggested_fix": { "type": "string" } }, "required": ["line", "severity", "category", "description"] } } }, "required": ["verdict", "issues"] } ``` --- ## 4. Comparison of Quality Control Approaches | Technique | Context Shared? | Catches Systematic Errors? | Execution Speed & Cost | Primary Use Case | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **[In-Context Self-Critique](../concepts/in-context-self-critique.md)** | Yes (Same turn) | ❌ Low (Confirmation bias) | Fast, Low cost | Quick surface-level formatting checks. | | **[Self-Consistency Sampling](../concepts/self-consistency-sampling.md)** | Yes (Parallel calls) | ❌ Low (Repeats majority errors) | Slow, High token cost | Simple math/factual queries with consensus targets. | | **Multi-Agent [Verifier Pattern](../concepts/verifier-pattern.md)** | ❌ No (Isolated) | ✅ High (Independent perspective) | Medium speed/cost | Code generation, document drafting, API payloads. | | **Sandboxed Compiler / [Formal Verification](../concepts/formal-verification.md)** | ❌ No (Deterministic) | ✅ Absolute (Mathematical proof) | Sub-second, Ultra-cheap | Financial rules, critical algorithms, type systems. | | **[Human-in-the-Loop Code Review](../concepts/human-in-the-loop-code-review.md)** | N/A | ✅ High | Slow, Manual bottleneck | Final pre-production sanity check on high-risk code. | --- ## 5. Core Implementation Rules for Harness Engineers 1. **Strict Context Stripping**: Never pass the builder's chain-of-thought, reasoning scratchpad, or intermediate tool outputs to the verifier agent. 2. **Operational Verification Criteria**: Provide specific, binary-evaluable test criteria rather than vague prompts ("find bugs"). 3. **Hard Bounded Retry Caps**: Set hard limits on builder-verifier loops (typically 3–5 iterations) to prevent runaway execution costs. 4. **Escalation & Fallback Protocols**: Define explicit fallback handlers (human review routing, warning logging) when retry caps are reached. --- ## 6. Verifier Model Selection Strategies ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph S1 ["Option 1: Same Model Baseline"] Builder1["Builder: Claude 3.5 Sonnet"] -->|Artifact Only| Verifier1["Verifier: Claude 3.5 Sonnet
(Fresh Context Window)"] end subgraph S2 ["Option 2: Heterogeneous Provider Pairing"] Builder2["Builder: GPT-4o"] -->|Artifact Only| Verifier2["Verifier: Claude 3.5 Sonnet
(Heterogeneous Reasoning & Datasets)"] end subgraph S3 ["Option 3: Asymmetric Tiered Pipeline"] Builder3["Builder: DeepSeek / Qwen"] -->|Artifact Only| Verifier3["Verifier: Claude 3.7 Sonnet / o1
(Heavy Reasoning Engine)"] end ``` | Strategy | Builder Model | Verifier Model | Best For | Architectural Rationale | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Homogeneous Baseline** | Same Model | Same Model (Fresh Context) | Internal scripts, standard features | Single API key, simple billing. Context isolation handles ~80% of confirmation bias. | | **Heterogeneous Pairing** | Provider A (e.g. GPT-4o) | Provider B (e.g. Claude 3.5 Sonnet) | High-stakes code, security, financial rules | **Zero shared model training bias**. Combines distinct reasoning architectures. | | **Asymmetric Tiered** | Fast / Cheap Model (DeepSeek, Qwen) | Heavy Reasoning Model (Claude 3.7, o1) | High-volume generation pipelines | Maximizes generation throughput while reserving expensive reasoning tokens for verification gates. | --- ## Related Links - Partition the domain into **[Bounded Contexts](../concepts/bounded-context.md)** and establish a shared **[Ubiquitous Language](../concepts/ubiquitous-language.md)** used across all specifications, code symbols, and team discussions. --- ### Stage 2: High-Level Roadmap & Capabilities Rather than creating hundreds of detailed micro-stories up front, business and engineering leaders define broad **Epics** or feature themes: - High-level capability definitions (e.g. *"Mobile Account Management"*, *"Payment Gateway Integration"*). - Establishes a functional roadmap without detailing specific UI widgets, API request schemas, or edge cases prematurely. --- ### Stage 3: Just-In-Time Story Refinement & Discovery 1 to 2 sprints prior to implementing a specific feature, the team refines Epics into actionable **[User Stories](../concepts/user-story.md)**: 1. **User Story Format**: - Formulated as `As an , I want , So that `. 2. **The Discovery Workshop ([Discovery Workshop](../concepts/discovery-workshop.md))**: - The **Three Amigos** (Product Owner, Developer, QA Tester) conduct a 25–30 minute structured conversation. 3. **Example Mapping**: - The team uses colored cards to map out the story: - 🟦 **Blue Card**: The User Story. - 🟨 **Yellow Cards**: Business Rules & Acceptance Criteria. - 🟩 **Green Cards**: Concrete real-world numerical or behavioral examples illustrating rules. - 🔴 **Red Cards**: Unanswered questions or missing facts requiring research spikes. --- ### Stage 4: Executable & Task Specification Formulation ([SDD](../concepts/spec-driven-development-sdd.md)) Green example cards from the Discovery Workshop are immediately translated into structured, machine-executable **[Gherkin](../concepts/gherkin.md)** `.feature` files and SDD task artifacts: 1. **Gherkin Executable Specifications**: ```gherkin Feature: Account Overdraft Protection Scenario: Deny transfer when source checking account is in overdraft Given my checking account has a balance of -$10.00 And my savings account has a balance of $100.00 When I attempt to transfer $20.00 from checking to savings Then the transfer should be denied And I should see an error message "Account is in overdraft" ``` 2. **SDD Task Specifications**: - Translating requirements into structured Markdown files (`requirements.md`, `design.md`, `tasks.md`) detailing input/output mappings, interface contracts, and preconditions. --- ### Stage 5: Context Assembly & Agentic Ingestion When initiating an AI-driven development turn, the **[Coding Agent](../concepts/coding-agent.md)** harness constructs an augmented prompt using a **Dual-Engine Retrieval Architecture** (see [Synthesis - Contextual Specification Ingestion for Coding Agents](synthesis-contextual-specification-ingestion-for-coding-agents.md)): 1. **Persistent Memory Bank Ingestion**: - Ingests the codebase **[Memory Bank](../concepts/memory-bank.md)** (`AGENTS.md`, `constitution.md`, `product.md`, `tech.md`) to enforce persistent system rules across all sessions. 2. **Specification Ingestion (Vector / Wiki RAG)**: - Ingests relevant [arc42](../concepts/arc42.md) architectural guardrails (*Context & Scope*, *Crosscutting Concepts*) and Gherkin `.feature` acceptance files. 3. **Code Context Ingestion (LSP & Tree-sitter)**: - Uses [LSP](../concepts/language-server-protocol-lsp.md) and [Tree-sitter](../concepts/tree-sitter.md) to construct accurate symbol graphs, type signatures, and definition-to-reference maps. 4. **Harness Prompt Assembly**: - Combines OS system instructions, available tool definitions (`read_file`, `edit_file`, `run_command`), Gherkin contract files, and codebase context into the model's working memory. --- ### Stage 6: Automated Execution & Maintenance Loop The AI **[Coding Agent](../concepts/coding-agent.md)** executes the implementation turn inside an autonomous harness loop: 1. **Initial Test Run (FAIL / RED)**: - The agent executes the Gherkin feature test suite via a BDD test runner (Cucumber / behave). The test fails as expected because the behavior is not yet implemented. 2. **Targeted Code Generation / Edits**: - The agent analyzes the failure output, reads relevant source files, and applies targeted edits using code editing tool primitives (`edit_file`). 3. **Automated Verification Loop ([Ralph Wiggum Loop](../concepts/ralph-wiggum-loop.md))**: - The harness re-executes the BDD test suite. If tests fail, the harness captures `stderr` feedback, appends it to the context, and instructs the agent to self-correct. 4. **SDD Maintenance Strategy**: - The team selects an explicit maintenance level for the created specification: - **Level 1 (Spec-First)**: Task spec is archived/discarded after implementation; code is maintained. - **Level 2 (Spec-Anchored)**: Task spec is retained in Git and evolved alongside code over feature lifetime. - **Level 3 (Spec-as-Source)**: Human edits *only* specs; source code is treated as a disposable compiled byproduct (`// GENERATED FROM SPEC`). --- ## Related Links - **Syntheses**: [Synthesis - Project Initialization Sequence](synthesis-project-initialization-sequence.md), [Synthesis - Based on precise observational data compiled by Tycho Brahe, these laws replaced circular epicycle models with elliptical orbits and later provided the empirical foundation for [Isaac Newton](../entities/isaac-newton.md)'s law of universal gravitation and modern [Orbital Mechanics](orbital-mechanics.md). --- ## The Three Laws ```mermaid flowchart TD KeplerLaws[Kepler's Three Laws] --> Law1["1st Law: Law of Ellipses
Orbits are ellipses with primary at one focus"] KeplerLaws --> Law2["2nd Law: Law of Equal Areas
Radius vector sweeps equal area in equal time"] KeplerLaws --> Law3["3rd Law: Law of Harmonics
Square of period is proportional to cube of semi-major axis"] ``` ### 1. First Law (The Law of Ellipses) > *All planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one of the two foci.* An ellipse is defined by its semi-major axis $a$ and eccentricity $e$. The distance from the focus to periapsis is $r_p = a(1-e)$ and to apoapsis is $r_a = a(1+e)$.[^migration-source-basics-of-space-flight-orbital-mechanics-0] ### 2. Second Law (The Law of Equal Areas) > *A line segment joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time.* This law implies that an orbiting body speeds up near periapsis (closest approach) and slows down near apoapsis (farthest distance), representing the conservation of angular momentum ($r v \sin\phi = \text{constant}$). ### 3. Third Law (The Law of Harmonics) > *The square of the orbital period of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit.* $$P^2 \propto a^3 \quad \implies \quad P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{\mu} a^3$$ Where $\mu = G(M + m) \approx GM$ for secondary masses negligible relative to the primary. --- ## Related Links - **Concepts**: [Orbital Mechanics](orbital-mechanics.md), [Hohmann Transfer Orbit](hohmann-transfer-orbit.md) - **Entities**: [Johannes Kepler](../entities/johannes-kepler.md), [Isaac Newton](../entities/isaac-newton.md) - **Sources**: [Source - Basics of Space Flight Orbital Mechanics](../sources/source-basics-of-space-flight-orbital-mechanics.md) ## Evidence & Citations - [Source Note](../sources/source-basics-of-space-flight-orbital-mechanics.md) [^migration-source-basics-of-space-flight-orbital-mechanics-0]: [Source Note](../sources/source-basics-of-space-flight-orbital-mechanics.md), claims matrix; [Raw File](../../raw/Basics%20of%20Space%20Flight%20Orbital%20Mechanics.md).

# Orbital Mechanics

## Definition & Overview
**Orbital Mechanics** (also called *Astrodynamics* or *Flight Mechanics*) is the application of ballistics and celestial mechanics to the practical problems concerning the motion of rockets, spacecraft, and artificial satellites under the influence of forces such as gravity, atmospheric drag, and propulsive thrust.

It evolved from classical celestial mechanics, pioneered by [Isaac Newton](../entities/isaac-newton.md) and [Johannes Kepler](../entities/johannes-kepler.md), into an applied engineering discipline covering ascent trajectories, orbit transfer maneuvers, rendezvous, atmospheric reentry, and interplanetary trajectories.[^migration-source-basics-of-space-flight-orbital-mechanics-0]

---

## Key Principles & Conic Trajectories

Orbital motion is modeled using two-body gravitational dynamics where a spacecraft moves along a conic section relative to a primary gravitating body.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OrbitalMotion[Orbital Trajectories] --> Bound[Bound Orbits: E < 0]
    OrbitalMotion --> Unbound[Unbound Trajectories: E ≥ 0]

    Bound --> Circular["Circular Orbit (e = 0)"]
    Bound --> Elliptical["Elliptical Orbit (0 < e < 1)"]
    
    Unbound --> Parabolic["Parabolic Escape (e = 1, E = 0)"]
    Unbound --> Hyperbolic["Hyperbolic Flyby (e > 1, E > 0)"]
```

### Governing Equations
- **Vis-Viva Energy Equation**:
  $$v^2 = \mu \left( \frac{2}{r} - \frac{1}{a} \right)$$
- **Orbital Period**:
  $$P = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a^3}{\mu}}$$
- **Escape Velocity**:
  $$v_{esc} = \sqrt{\frac{2\mu}{r}}$$

---

## Core Engineering Domains
1. **Keplerian Element Definition**: Defining 3D space orientation ($a, e, i, \omega, T, \Omega$).
2. **Orbital Maneuvering**: In-plane altitude transfers via [Hohmann Transfer Orbit](hohmann-transfer-orbit.md), One-Tangent burns, or low-thrust spirals, and out-of-plane inclination changes.
3. **Perturbation Analysis**: Accounting for non-spherical Earth oblateness ($J_2$), atmospheric drag, third-body gravity (Sun/Moon), and solar radiation pressure. The [Lagrange Points](lagrange-points.md) concept provides a related three-body rotating-frame model.
4. **Interplanetary Trajectories**: Managing launch windows, hyperbolic excess velocity ($v_\infty$), and planetary spheres of influence ($r_{SOI}$).

---

# Lagrange Points

> [!WARNING]
> **Evidence Status:** Seed synthesis — no raw source has been ingested yet. Treat this as a working mental model, not a source-backed finding.

## Definition

**Lagrange points** are five positions in the idealized circular restricted three-body problem where the gravitational influence of two primary bodies and the apparent centrifugal effect in their rotating frame balance so that a negligible-mass third body can share the primaries' angular motion. The third body is not gravity-free or motionless; it is continuously accelerating with the rotating system.

This extends the usual two-body approximation used in [Orbital Mechanics](orbital-mechanics.md) by treating the gravity of two primaries and a rotating reference frame together.

## The Five Points

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    PrimaryA[Primary A] --- L1[L1: between primaries] --- PrimaryB[Primary B]
    PrimaryB --- L2[L2: beyond smaller primary]
    PrimaryA --- L3[L3: beyond larger primary]
    L4[L4: 60 degrees ahead] --- PrimaryA
    L4 --- PrimaryB
    L5[L5: 60 degrees behind] --- PrimaryA
    L5 --- PrimaryB
```

- **L1** lies between the primaries. It is useful when a spacecraft must observe or communicate with the nearer primary while remaining aligned with both bodies.
- **L2** lies beyond the smaller primary on the line joining the primaries. A spacecraft there can remain approximately aligned with the smaller primary as both orbit their common center of mass.
- **L3** lies beyond the larger primary, opposite the smaller primary, and is generally less convenient for communications and operations.
- **L4** and **L5** lead and trail the smaller primary by roughly 60 degrees. Together with the primaries, each forms an approximately equilateral triangle.

## Stability and Mission Design

L1, L2, and L3 are equilibrium locations in the idealized rotating model but are not generally passively stable. Missions near them commonly use halo or Lissajous orbits rather than attempting to remain exactly at a mathematical point, and they require station-keeping to correct for perturbations and navigation error.

L4 and L5 can be dynamically stable for suitable primary mass ratios, allowing objects to librate around those regions. Stability is a property of the full system model, not a guarantee that every object placed near a point will remain there indefinitely.

## Connections

Lagrange-point analysis is a three-body extension of [Orbital Mechanics](orbital-mechanics.md), contrasting with the simpler two-body conic trajectories used for many first-order mission calculations. It also complements [Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion](kepler-s-laws-of-planetary-motion.md) by describing motion in a rotating system rather than a single-primary ellipse.

## Open Questions

- What equations and numerical methods best locate the points in an elliptic, non-ideal primary system?
- How do halo and Lissajous orbit families differ in station-keeping cost and communication geometry?
- What dedicated source should be ingested to replace this seed synthesis with source-backed claims and precise stability criteria?

- **Published**: 2005-12-06
- **Source URL**: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultrasonic_transducer

## High-Level Summary
This article provides an overview of ultrasonic transducers and sensors—devices that generate or detect ultrasonic energy (sound waves above 20 kHz). It details the primary categories (transmitters, receivers, transceivers), core underlying physical mechanisms (piezoelectric, capacitive, magnetostrictive, MEMS-based MUTs), and wide-ranging applications in medical imaging, depth sounding, sonomicrometry, and obstacle ranging.

## Core Takeaways

### 1. Classification & Conversion Principles
* **Transmitters**: Convert electrical energy/AC signals into ultrasonic acoustic waves.
* **Receivers**: Convert incoming ultrasonic waves into measurable electrical signals.
* **Transceivers**: Combined devices capable of both transmitting and receiving ultrasound pulses.

### 2. Transducer Technologies & Mechanisms
* **Piezoelectric Transducers**: Utilize materials that deform in response to applied voltage (and generate voltage when mechanically strained).
* **Capacitive Transducers**: Utilize electrostatic fields between a flexible conductive diaphragm and a fixed backplate.
* **Magnetostrictive Transducers**: Rely on materials that change dimensions when exposed to magnetic fields.
* **[Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducers (MUTs)](../concepts/micromachined-ultrasonic-transducer-mut.md)**: Fabricated using silicon MEMS technology to create compact array sensors. Includes **CMUT** (capacitive), **PMUT** (piezoelectric), and **OMUS** (optical ring resonator sensors).

### 3. Key Applications
* **Distance Ranging & Sonomicrometry**: Measuring time-of-flight (ToF) of acoustic bursts between transducers for high-precision spatial positioning.
* **Depth Sounding / Sonar**: Echosounding to measure water depth (e.g., fathometers) using sound speed in water (~1.5 km/s).
* **Medical Ultrasonography**: Non-invasive 2D/3D cross-sectional imaging probes and modern wearable continuous-monitoring ultrasound patches.
* **Industrial & Environmental**: Fluid level sensing, anemometers (wind speed), acoustic levitation, and non-destructive material testing.

# Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer (MUT)

A **Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer (MUT)** is an [Ultrasonic Transducer](ultrasonic-transducer.md) fabricated using micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) silicon manufacturing technology.[^migration-source-ultrasonic-transducer-0]

MEMS fabrication allows thousands of microscopic transducer elements to be integrated onto a single silicon chip, enabling compact, high-resolution transducer arrays for medical imaging, industrial sensors, and consumer electronics.

## Primary Types

1. **CMUT (Capacitive Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer)**: Uses electrostatic fields between a flexible micromachined silicon membrane and a fixed backing plate.
2. **PMUT (Piezoelectric Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer)**: Integrates a thin piezoelectric film (such as PZT or AlN) directly onto a vibrating silicon membrane.
3. **OMUS (Optical Micro-machined Ultrasound Sensor)**: Utilizes integrated silicon photonic optical ring resonators inside a membrane to detect acoustic strain via optical wavelength shifts.

## Advantages
* **Miniaturization**: Small footprint allowing integration into wearable patches or compact robotic arrays.
* **Array Density**: Easy batch fabrication of 1D and 2D phased arrays.
* **Acoustic Impedance Matching**: Offers better acoustic impedance matching to air and water compared to bulk ceramic transducers.

# Source - Wave Function Collapse Explained

- **Title**: Wave Function Collapse Explained
- **Author**: [Boris](../entities/boris.md)
- **Published**: 2020-04-13
- **Source URL**: https://www.boristhebrave.com/2020/04/13/wave-function-collapse-explained/

## High-Level Summary
This article outlines the fundamentals of the Wave Function Collapse ([WFC](../concepts/wave-function-collapse.md)) algorithm and how it builds on [Constraint Programming](../concepts/constraint-programming.md). Rather than a quantum physics concept, WFC is a constraint-solving method optimized to procedurally generate tile-based layouts or images from a set of rules or source examples.

## Core Takeaways

### 1. Constraint Programming Foundations
* Unlike imperative or functional programming, **Constraint Programming** involves specifying a problem by defining:
  * **Variables**: Unknown values to solve.
  * **Domain**: The set of permissible values for each variable.
  * **Constraints**: Rules relating variables together (e.g., `all_distinct`).
* **Constraint Propagation**: Information passes from one variable to another via constraints, systematically shrinking domains.
* **Backtracking**: When a puzzle reaches a state where a cell has an empty domain (a contradiction), the algorithm backtracks to the last valid guess state, eliminates the failed guess, and tries a different value.

### 2. Wave Function Collapse (WFC) Mechanics
* Developed by [Maxim Gumin](../entities/maxim-gumin.md) based on Paul Merrell's model synthesis, WFC is a generator rather than a solver because it resolves choices using random selections under constraint rules.
* **Basic WFC Loop**:
  1. Initialize each grid cell's domain with all possible tiles (boolean array set to true).
  2. Pick the un-collapsed cell with the **least entropy** (fewest remaining tile choices).
  3. Force a random selection (observation) on that cell, removing all other tiles from its domain.
  4. Run **constraint propagation** recursively to update the domains of adjacent/impacted cells.
  5. Repeat until all cells have a domain of size 1 (collapsed).
* Under a sensible tileset, WFC rarely needs to backtrack, allowing the backtracking steps to be omitted for simple runs.

### 3. Key WFC Optimizations
* **Queue-based Propagation**: Maintain a queue of modified cells, only re-evaluating constraints on cells adjacent to those that changed, preventing redundant loops.
* **Support Counts**: Keep a multidimensional tracking array counting how many compatible neighbors a given tile has on each side. A tile's entry is marked impossible immediately when its support count on any edge drops to zero.

### 4. Advanced Variations
* **Hex/3D Topologies**: WFC operates on any geometric graph.
* **Overlapped WFC**: Instead of basic adjacency rules, WFC copies 3x3 pixel/tile patterns observed in a sample image. This captures larger relationships (e.g., green tiles near blue tiles, but never adjacent) but is computationally heavier.

# Kubernetes Architecture

**Kubernetes Architecture** defines the structural separation of concerns in a Kubernetes cluster between the **Master Node (Control Plane)**, which manages global cluster state and scheduling decisions, and **Worker Nodes**, which host and run containerized application workloads.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           MASTER NODE                             |
|  +--------------------+  +---------------+  +------------------+  |
|  | API Server         |  | Scheduler     |  | Controller Mgrs  |  |
|  | (kube-apiserver)   |  | (kube-sched)  |  | (Kube & Cloud)   |  |
|  +---------+----------+  +-------+-------+  +--------+---------+  |
|            |                     |                   |            |
|            +---------------------+-------------------+            |
|                                  |                                |
|                           +------+------+                         |
|                           |    etcd     |                         |
|                           +-------------+                         |
+----------------------------------+--------------------------------+
                                   |
              +--------------------+--------------------+
              |                                         |
+-------------v-------------------+       +-------------v-------------------+
|          WORKER NODE 1          |       |          WORKER NODE 2          |
|  +--------------+ +----------+  |       |  +--------------+ +----------+  |
|  | Kubelet      | | Kube     |  |       |  | Kubelet      | | Kube     |  |
|  |              | | Proxy    |  |       |  |              | | Proxy    |  |
|  +-------+------+ +----+-----+  |       |  +-------+------+ +----+-----+  |
|          |             |        |       |          |             |        |
|  +-------v-------------v-----+  |       |  +-------v-------------v-----+  |
|  | Container Runtime (CRI)   |  |       |  | Container Runtime (CRI)   |  |
|  | +-----------------------+ |  |       |  | +-----------------------+ |  |
|  | | Pods & Containers     | |  |       |  | | Pods & Containers     | |  |
|  | +-----------------------+ |  |       |  | +-----------------------+ |  |
|  +---------------------------+  |       |  +---------------------------+  |
+---------------------------------+       +---------------------------------+
```

## 1. Master Node Components (Control Plane)
The Master Node maintains cluster state and responds to declarative API specifications (as outlined in [Source - Getting Started with Kubernetes](../sources/source-getting-started-with-kubernetes.md)):
* **API Server (`kube-apiserver`)**: The central RESTful interface for all administrative commands (`kubectl`), worker nodes, and internal controllers.
* **Scheduler (`kube-scheduler`)**: Evaluates workload requirements (CPU, memory, constraints) and assigns unassigned Pods to optimal worker nodes.
* **Kube Controller Manager (`kube-controller-manager`)**: Runs reconciliation loops (Node Controller, ReplicaSet Controller, Endpoints Controller, Service Account Controller) to align current state with desired state.
* **Cloud Controller Manager (`cloud-controller-manager`)**: Optional component interfacing with external cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure) to manage cloud storage, routes, and load balancers.
* **etcd**: Distributed, high-availability key-value store holding the complete persistence layer and operational state of the cluster.[^migration-source-getting-started-with-kubernetes-0]

## 2. Worker Node Components
Worker Nodes provide computing capacity and host container runtimes:
* **Kubelet**: The primary node daemon communicating with the API Server. Registers node resources, receives Pod specifications, and delegates container execution to the Container Runtime.
* **Container Runtime (CRI)**: Software underlying container execution (e.g., Docker, `containerd`, `cri-o`). Interfaced via the Container Runtime Interface.
* **Kube Proxy (`kube-proxy`)**: Maintained network proxy reflecting Kubernetes Service definitions on each node by performing IP and port forwarding (via iptables or IPVS).
* **Pods**: The fundamental runtime units hosting application containers.

# Immutable Core and Mutable Shell

**Immutable Core and Mutable Shell** is a functional software architecture pattern detailed by [Vladimir Khorikov](../entities/vladimir-khorikov.md) in [Source - Immutable Architecture (Khorikov)](../sources/source-immutable-architecture-khorikov.md). It isolates side-effect-free domain logic into a pure mathematical core while delegating I/O and state persistence to a simple, low-complexity shell.

---

## Architectural Breakdown

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MUTABLE SHELL (Dumb I/O & Persistence)                       │
│ - Cyclomatic Complexity = 1 (No conditional logic)          │
│ - Reads input data -> Passes to Core                       │
│ - Receives Action Artifacts -> Applies DB/Disk changes     │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                               │
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ IMMUTABLE CORE (Pure Functional Domain Logic)               │
│ - Side-effect free (Mathematical functions)                 │
│ - Highly testable (No mock databases/files needed)          │
│ - Accepts FileContent/Inputs -> Emits FileAction/Artifacts  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

1. **Immutable Core**:
   * Contains all domain rules.
   * Functions accept input parameters and return action objects/artifacts (e.g., `FileAction`, `Command`) without mutating state or performing I/O operations.
   * Enables trivial unit testing (input $\rightarrow$ expected output verification without mocking file systems or databases).
2. **Mutable Shell**:
   * Responsible solely for reading inputs from databases/files and writing the core's output artifacts to storage at the end of the transaction.
   * Designed with minimal cyclomatic complexity (ideally 1, containing no conditional `if` logic).[^migration-source-immutable-architecture-khorikov-0]
